title: Find all duplicates in an array (index-marking or frequency map).
shortTitle: Find All Duplicates in an Array: Index-Marking or Frequency Map
keyPoints: A frequency HashMap counts occurrences and collects keys with count 2 or more in O(n) time and O(n) space.
Index-marking works only when values are in range 1 to n: negate the element at the index encoded by each value.
If the target slot is already negative, the value is a duplicate; use absolute value when computing the target index.
Index-marking achieves O(n) time with O(1) extra space by storing the seen flag in the sign bit of the array.
Restore the array afterward by taking absolute values if the caller needs the original data.
Choose frequency map when the range constraint fails or mutation is forbidden; choose marking when the constraint holds and memory is tight.
In banking, this detects double-charged transaction references in a daily batch.

s1_definition.oneliner: Count with a frequency map, or when values are one to n, flip the sign at the indexed slot and a pre-flipped slot means a duplicate.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Frequency map approach** – use a `HashMap<Integer, Integer>` to count occurrences, collecting keys with count >= 2 in O(n) time and O(n) space.
- **Index-marking approach** – valid when values are in `[1, n]`; for each value `v`, negate `a[|v| - 1]`; if it is already negative, `v` is a duplicate. O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
- **Absolute value** – always use `Math.abs(a[i])` when computing the target index because the element may have been negated by an earlier visit.
- **Array restoration** – after collecting duplicates, take absolute values to undo the marks if the caller needs the original array.
- **Choice** – frequency map for arbitrary values or immutable arrays; index-marking for `[1, n]` constraint with mutation allowed.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India processes a batch of transaction reference numbers and the fraud team must spot every reference that appears more than once, since duplicates can mean a double-charge. The simple way is a tally sheet (HashMap). The clever way, when references are numbered 1 to batch-size, is to flip a mark at the slot each reference points to, and if that slot is already flipped, the reference is a repeat.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding all duplicates reports every value that appears more than once, and you pick one of two approaches depending on the constraints. The general approach is a frequency map: walk the array once, increment each value's count, and collect a value the instant its count reaches exactly two. That is O(n) time and O(n) space and works for any values.

When the problem guarantees every value lies in the range 1 to n and allows mutation, index-marking drops the extra space to O(1). For each value, compute a target index as the absolute value minus one, check the element there: if it is already negative, an earlier value pointed here so this is a duplicate, otherwise negate it to mark it seen. The absolute value step is essential because the element you inspect may have been negated earlier.

The responsibility you always call out is restoring the array. Negating mutates the caller's input, so if the original values are needed afterward, walk the array and take absolute values. Silently corrupting a caller's data is a real production bug.

In a banking project at the National Bank of India, the fraud team uses this to flag every transaction reference that appeared more than once in a daily batch, which can signal a double-charge, using the map for arbitrary reference strings and index-marking for batches numbered 1 to size.

Remember one sentence: Use a frequency map for general duplicates, or negate elements at value-derived indices for O(1) space when values are in [1, n].
